clues.title: Plate: white front, yellow back
text: UK front plates are **white**, while back plates are **yellow**. Some plates have a blue strip on the left, but most do not.
Additionally, you might see a plate with a **green **[‘Zero Emissions’](/images/united-kingdom/UK_Zero_Emission_License_Plate.png) strip.
NOTE: Ireland uses white front and back plates, always with a blue strip on the left.

images.caption: British plates: white front and yellow rear, old and new styles

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Front plates are white and back plates yellow. Most have no blue strip, some have a green Zero Emissions strip. Irish plates are white front and back with a blue strip.

differs.how: Irish plates are white both ends, always with blue strip

clues.title: Driving side: left
text: The UK drives on the **left side** of the road.
NOTE: The UK, Ireland, Malta and Cyprus are the only European countries that drive on the left.

images.caption: A British road with traffic driving on the left; the added sign shows two-way traffic

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Drives on the left. Ireland, Malta and Cyprus are the only other European countries that do.

clues.title: Road lines: double yellow at the edge
text: **Double yellow road lines** are often found on the sides of marked roads, especially in urban areas. These lines indicate a no stopping zone.
NOTE: These lines can also be found in Ireland.

images.caption: Red circle and arrow zoom in on the double yellow lines at the road edge

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Double yellow lines along the edge of marked roads, mainly in towns, mean no stopping. Also found in Ireland.

clues.title: Road lines: long dashes with cat's eyes between
text: These middle lines, that consist of** long dashes **with** cat’s eyes **(reflectors) in the gaps between the dashes, are a good clue for the UK.

images.caption: Red arrow points to a cat's eye reflector set between the long centre dashes
Red arrow points to a cat's eye reflector set between the long centre dashes

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A middle line of long dashes with reflectors (cat's eyes) in the gaps is a good clue.

clues.title: Bollard: rounded, black ends, white stripe
text: The most common **bollard** in the UK looks like this. It has a rounded shape, with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back. The base and top are black, with a white stripe in the middle.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The most common bollard: rounded, black base and top with a white stripe in the middle, a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back.

clues.title: Pole: wooden with metal step rods
text: The UK uses **wooden** poles. Pole steps bolted on the side of the pole are very common. These pole steps are shaped like a series of thin horizontal metal rods.
NOTE: Ireland also commonly uses wooden poles with pole steps.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Wooden poles, often with thin horizontal metal rods bolted on as steps. Ireland has the same.

clues.title: Pole: wooden with metal crossbar triangle
text: Poles in the UK occasionally have a **metal crossbar** near the top with two diagonal supports forming a triangle shape.
NOTE: Ireland, as well as Sweden and Finland also use similar crossbars on some poles.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Poles sometimes have a metal crossbar near the top with two diagonal supports forming a triangle. Ireland, Sweden and Finland have similar ones.

clues.title: Chevron: black with white arrows
text: Chevrons are **black with white arrows**.
NOTE: Irish chevrons are black with yellow arrows. French chevrons are blue with white arrows.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Black chevrons with white arrows. Irish ones are black with yellow arrows, French ones blue with white.

differs.how: French chevrons are blue with white arrows

clues.title: Sign: red-bordered triangle warning signs
text: Like most European countries, the UK uses **triangular warning signs** with a red border and a white background.
NOTE: This is mostly useful to distinguish between the UK and Ireland, as Ireland uses diamond-shaped yellow warning signs (being the only European country to do so).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Triangular warning signs with a red border and white background, as in most of Europe. Ireland uses yellow diamonds.

differs.how: Irish warning signs are yellow diamonds

clues.title: Direction sign: blue, green or white with A or M
text: Direction signs in the United Kingdom can be **blue, green, or white.** Look for the letters **A** or **M**, as these are the major roads in the country. Smaller roads start with **B**.
NOTE: Irish direction signs are typically bilingual, with Irish names in italics, making them easy to distinguish from the UK ones.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Direction signs can be blue, green or white. A and M are major roads, B smaller ones. Irish signs are bilingual with Irish names in italics.

differs.how: Irish signs are bilingual, Irish in italics

clues.title: Street sign: low white sign on two posts
text: The UK commonly uses these **white street signs** with black text, that are positioned low to the ground. They are usually supported by two small posts. Many street signs in suburban areas will have a small cul-de-sac icon.
They can sometimes have [different colours](https://goo.gl/maps/Uc9Wf1fjrpvfSTBM8) or feature small designs, like [coats of arms](https://goo.gl/maps/8Di7Wx8TC3dvs8gKA).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: White street signs with black text, placed low to the ground on two small posts. Suburban ones often have a small cul-de-sac icon. Some have other colours or crests.

clues.title: Sign: give way sign says GIVE WAY
text: UK yield signs feature the phrase “**GIVE WAY**”.
NOTE: [Irish yields signs](https://goo.gl/maps/GAm9QdSeKWWahHny5) just have the word “YIELD”.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Yield signs say GIVE WAY. Irish ones say YIELD.

clues.title: Pole: yellow sticker with a person being zapped
text: The **yellow warning stickers** on utility poles can be a good way to distinguish between the UK and Ireland.
The most important difference is that UK stickers feature a guy getting zapped by a lightning bolt.

The [Irish stickers](https://goo.gl/maps/bzrUc5Wo1QrrhxD76) usually have a lightning bolt, but lack the guy getting zapped. They also often have an extra second rectangular sticker with a black outline, below the lightning bolt.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Yellow warning stickers on poles show a person hit by a lightning bolt. Irish ones usually show just a bolt, often with an extra black-outlined sticker below.

differs.how: Irish stickers have no zapped person

clues.title: Bollard: yellow
text: This **yellow traffic bollard** is commonly found in the UK.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A yellow traffic bollard is commonly found.

clues.title: Sign: black-white striped post with yellow bulb
text: Pedestrian crossing signs are almost non-existent in the UK. Instead, pedestrian crossings will often have these distinctive **black and white striped poles**, with a yellow light bulb on top.
NOTE: These signposts are also common in Ireland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Pedestrian crossings are marked by a black-and-white striped post with a yellow bulb on top, not a sign. Very common in Ireland too.

clues.title: Farm gate: square corners
text: Rural metal gates with **square corners** are very common in the UK.

NOTE: This is mainly useful to distinguish it from [Ireland](https://goo.gl/maps/7LXuTr1R1Fv6L8tg8), where similar gates typically have rounded corners. Gates in [Northern Ireland](https://goo.gl/maps/y1AK7sL8MgoDdmVm9) also typically have rounded corners.

images.caption: A farm gate with square corners; the red circle zooms in on the corner

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Rural metal gates have square corners. Irish gates usually have rounded corners, and Northern Ireland's do too.

differs.how: Irish farm gates have rounded corners

clues.title: Landscape: green fields, hedgerows, low hills
text: The British countryside tends to be very green, with lots of **hedgerows **lining the road. Low, rolling hills are common throughout most of the country.
NOTE: The Irish countryside looks very similar, so make sure to look at other clues before guessing.

images.caption: A narrow road between tall green hedges and flat farmland

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Very green countryside with many hedgerows beside the road and low rolling hills. Ireland looks very similar.

clues.title: Houses: terraced and semi-detached rows
text: **Terraced houses** (row houses) are very common in the UK. This housing type shares walls on both sides with neighbouring homes. You will also see a lot of [semi-detached houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-detached), which share just one side wall with another house.

NOTE: [61% of the population](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/ILC_LVHO01__custom_4934075/default/table?lang=en) lives in terraced or semi-detached houses, significantly more than most other European countries. The only European countries where terraced houses are this common are Ireland and the Netherlands.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Terraced houses (rows sharing both side walls) and semi-detached houses (sharing one wall) are very common; about 61% of people live in them. Only Ireland and the Netherlands are similar in Europe.

clues.title: Houses: red brick
text: **Red brick buildings **are common in many parts of the UK.
NOTE: Red brick architecture is also common in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Denmark, as well as parts of northern France.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Red brick buildings are common in many parts. Also common in the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark and parts of northern France.

clues.title: Houses: identical suburban semis, cul-de-sacs
text: **Suburbs** in UK towns tend to have a recognizable look. They typically feature near-identical houses, often semi-detached, usually with [well-manicured lawns](https://goo.gl/maps/Am191RdWfDF927Rt8). The road layout can be maze-like, with lots of cul-de-sacs and curvy roads.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Suburbs have near-identical, often semi-detached houses with neat lawns and a maze of cul-de-sacs and curvy roads.

clues.title: Houses: chimney with several round pots
text: Many British buildings have distinct-looking chimneys with multiple so-called **chimney pots**. These pots are usually round and brick-coloured.

images.caption: Chimney with several round pots; the red arrow points to the chimney pots

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Many buildings have chimneys topped with several round, brick-coloured pots.

clues.title: Houses: black-and-white timber framing
text: Some buildings, both old and new, feature [black-and-white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black-and-white_Revival_architecture) **timber framing**.
NOTE: This is less common in Ireland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some old and new buildings have black-and-white timber framing. Less common in Ireland.

clues.title: Coverage: low camera, big round blur
text: The UK has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.

images.caption: Four panels labelled front panned down, front panned straight, back panned down and good blur (front)

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A low-mounted Gen 4 camera with a big round blur and a small bump at the front. The blur can be see-through, which makes it easy to miss.

clues.title: Flags: the four national flags
text: Occasionally, you can find one of the **4 country flags**, which will tell you where in the UK you are.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: You sometimes see one of the four national flags, which tells you which part you are in.

clues.title: Route marker: first digit shows the area
text: **A- and B-roads** are **grouped** by their first digit, for example A380 and B3217 are located in the southwest of the country. Motorways also generally follow this pattern.
Beware that roads starting with any digit from 1 to 8 can also be found in Northern Ireland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A- and B-roads are grouped by first digit, so A380 and B3217 are in the southwest. Motorways follow the pattern. Think of a clock: digits go clockwise from 1 to 9. Roads starting 1 to 8 can also be in Northern Ireland.

clues.title: Phone numbers: area codes, 020 and 028
text: **Landline phone numbers** in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.
A complete overview of all other area codes is available in [this infographic](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3d/Map_of_the_Telephone_Dialling_Codes_in_the_United_Kingdom.png).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Landlines have nine or ten digits after the 0, and the first two to four are the area code. Geography is mostly random, but big-city codes are worth learning. All of London uses 020 and all of Northern Ireland 028.

clues.title: Bin: city name on it
text: Bins in urban areas often have the **city name** on them.

images.caption: Two bins with a council name; the red circle and arrow point to the logo

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bins in towns often have the city name written on them.

clues.title: Landscape: barren high mountains
text: The Scottish Highlands can be distinguished by the semi-barren, very **mountainous** landscape.
NOTE: A lot of Generation 4 coverage in the Highlands is from (early) spring, meaning that the vegetation often looks brown and yellow.
In addition, some of the most mountainous parts of [Wales](https://goo.gl/maps/DZCbKEo8L9PGxqDG9) and [Northern England](https://goo.gl/maps/RdTAYzq7X8exyYGx7) can look similar.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The Scottish Highlands are semi-barren and very mountainous. Much Gen 4 coverage is from early spring, so plants look brown and yellow. The most mountainous parts of Wales and northern England can look similar.

clues.title: Bollard: round red-white with red-grey reflector
text: In Scotland, you can often find these **red and white bollards**. They are round, bulky, and have a red-and-grey reflector that wraps all the way around.
They are sometimes found in other parts of the UK.
NOTE: The bollard looks similar to the French one. However, there are some small differences. For example, the Scottish bollard is round on the top, while the French one is more spiked.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Common in Scotland: a round, bulky red-and-white bollard with a red-and-grey reflector wrapping all the way round, sometimes elsewhere. Looks like a French one but its top is round, not spiked.

differs.how: French bollard top is more spiked

clues.title: Sign: diamond Passing Place sign
text: These** diamond-shaped** **‘Passing Place’ **signs are most commonly found in Scotland.

images.caption: A white diamond Passing Place sign on a post

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Diamond-shaped Passing Place signs are mostly found in Scotland.

clues.title: Language: Welsh, many D, W, Y and LL
text: **Welsh** is a Celtic language that is spoken throughout Wales. Road signs in Wales are usually bilingual English and Welsh. Towns often have Welsh names too.
Welsh uses the letters **D**, **W**, and **Y** much more commonly than English. The double **LL** is also very distinct.
NOTE: Scottish Gaelic and Irish are both also Celtic languages. They can look somewhat similar to Welsh.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Welsh is spoken across Wales and road signs are usually bilingual. It uses D, W and Y a lot, and the double LL is distinct. Scottish Gaelic and Irish look somewhat similar.

differs.how: Irish is a different Celtic language that looks similar

clues.title: Road marking: ARAF written in Welsh
text: In Wales, markings on the road are in both English and Welsh. One of the best examples of this is ‘**Araf**’, which means ‘Slow’. This marking is only found in Wales.

NOTE: Araf is not the only Welsh language marking you can find, it is just the most common. Whenever you see an [obviously non-English](https://goo.gl/maps/zqv7eS2fjFDEjS2f8) marking next to an English one, consider guessing in Wales.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Road markings are in English and Welsh. ARAF (Slow) is the most common and only found in Wales. Any clearly non-English marking next to an English one points to Wales.

clues.title: Language: Gaelic clusters bh, dh, fh, mh
text: **Scottish Gaelic** is a Celtic language that is closely related to Irish. They have a very similar look and use accent marks commonly. Common and recognizable letter clusters include bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo, and ui.
Scottish Gaelic on road signs is found most commonly in the Scottish Highlands, and is almost always found north of Glasgow.
NOTE: Scottish Gaelic on road signs will often be in green or yellow text. This will not happen with Welsh or Irish on road signs.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Scottish Gaelic is closely related to Irish and uses accents. Look for bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo and ui. On road signs it is mostly in the Highlands, north of Glasgow, and often in green or yellow text, which Welsh and Irish signs never use.

differs.how: Irish signs are never in green or yellow text

clues.title: Houses: big blocks of sandstone or granite
text: It is common to see houses made of **large blocks of sandstone or granite **in Scotland. [Granite](https://goo.gl/maps/wYZvi7P1M195vc5N9) buildings are common in Aberdeen, [red sandstone](https://goo.gl/maps/k4HthFRKwCX4hQt8A) is common in Glasgow and Dumfries, and [yellow sandstone](https://goo.gl/maps/7TNfGv5GGmDqErA77) is common in Edinburgh.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Houses of large sandstone or granite blocks are common in Scotland. Granite in Aberdeen, red sandstone in Glasgow and Dumfries, yellow sandstone in Edinburgh.

clues.title: Plants: Cornish palm
text: Cornish palms (_Cordyline australis_) in the UK are most commonly found in the far **southwest** along the coast and in Jersey. Although, they can rarely be found all along the west coast up to Scotland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Cornish palms (Cordyline australis) are most common in the far southwest along the coast and in Jersey, and rarely up the west coast to Scotland.

clues.title: Lamppost: black sticker with yellow text
text: These **black stickers with yellow text** sometimes appear on lampposts in Northern Ireland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Black stickers with yellow text sometimes appear on lampposts in Northern Ireland. Wiltshire has the same stickers.

clues.title: Pole: warning stickers wrapped around the pole
text: Warning stickers **wrapped** all the way around the utility pole are specific to Northern Ireland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Warning stickers wrapped all the way around the pole are specific to Northern Ireland. Mainland poles usually have one or two stickers.

clues.title: Coverage: Gen 2 only on an island
text: The Isle of Man is an island in the Irish Sea between the United Kingdom and Ireland. There is only **Generation 2** coverage on the island. For country streak purposes, it is counted as part of the United Kingdom.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to the Isle of Man [here](https://www.plonkit.net/isle-of-man).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The Isle of Man, between Britain and Ireland, only has Gen 2 coverage. It counts as the UK for country streaks.

clues.title: Coverage: Gen 2 only on a Channel island
text: Jersey is an island in the English Channel between France and England. There is only **Generation 2** coverage on the island. For country streak purposes, it is counted as part of the United Kingdom.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Jersey [here](https://www.plonkit.net/jersey).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Jersey, between France and England, only has Gen 2 coverage. It counts as the UK for country streaks.

clues.title: Coverage: territory bordering Spain
text: Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory located at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, bordering Spain. For country streak purposes, the territory is counted as part of the United Kingdom.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Gibraltar [here](https://www.plonkit.net/gibraltar).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory at the southern tip of Iberia, bordering Spain. It counts as the UK for country streaks.

clues.title: Landscape: very hilly with bare rock, stone walls
text: The **Lake District** is very hilly, with a lot of exposed rocks and stone walls. It can look like the Scottish Highlands, but Scotland is generally less rocky.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The Lake District is very hilly with lots of exposed rock and stone walls. It can look like the Scottish Highlands, which are usually less rocky.

clues.title: Street sign: black name, red postcode and borough
text: **London street signs **have a distinct look. They usually feature the street name in black, followed by the postcode and borough in red.

images.caption: Churton Street sign with black name, red postcode and the borough name beneath

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: London signs show the street name in black, followed by the postcode and borough in red.

clues.title: Street sign: plain blue with white letters
text: Street name signs in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire typically feature a simple **blue background** with white lettering.
NOTE: Central Aberdeen uses a different, [black-and-yellow](https://maps.app.goo.gl/dpw9AUQ1e6ieL5U19) design.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Street signs in Aberdeen and Aberdeenshire are plain blue with white lettering. Central Aberdeen uses a black-and-yellow design.

clues.title: Street sign: green townland line under the name
text: Signs with **green text** underneath the street name, indicating the townland, can be found in the western part of Northern Ireland.
Especially towards the north of the shaded area, there may be a metal [divider](https://maps.app.goo.gl/AzvWFf8dyeHwbrp98) between the two lines.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Signs with green text under the street name (the townland) are in western Northern Ireland, sometimes with a metal divider between the two lines in the north.

clues.title: Street sign: black, white outline, Rockwell font
text: Most street signs in the Wakefield council are black with a white outline and letters. They use the Monotype Rockwell Nova font.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most street signs in the Wakefield council area are black with a white outline and letters, in the Monotype Rockwell Nova font.

clues.title: Google car: white electric car, back visible
text: Some of the Generation 4 coverage in London was taken by a **white electric vehicle**, with this distinct back of the car visible.
NOTE: A similar car was used in [Dublin](https://goo.gl/maps/1qo5Ymw2jADggdGX7) and [Germany](https://goo.gl/maps/za6Ex8aWnE5wsz3C7), so make sure to check out other clues as well.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some Gen 4 coverage in London was taken by a white electric car with a distinct back. Similar cars were used in Dublin and Germany.

clues.title: Pole: yellow tape or paint
text: The majority of poles and signposts in Birmingham have either **yellow tape** or yellow paint wrapped around them. Lampposts will also usually have this yellow sticker.

images.caption: A red circle zooms in on the yellow-and-black stripes and sticker on the pole

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most poles and signposts in Birmingham have yellow tape or paint wrapped around them. Lampposts usually have the yellow sticker too.

clues.title: Sign: Twenty’s Plenty speed sign, green border
text: Speed signs with green borders with the text “**Twenty’s Plenty**” are mostly found in and around Glasgow.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Speed signs with a green border and the words Twenty's Plenty are mostly in and around Glasgow.

clues.title: Bus stop: light blue UlsterBus sign
text: In Northern Ireland, most bus stops will have light blue UlsterBus signs.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In Northern Ireland, most bus stops have light blue UlsterBus signs.

clues.title: Pole: wooden pole with flat top
text: It is sometimes hard to distinguish France, Ireland, and the UK. An easy trick is to focus on the tops of the wooden poles: UK has a flat top

images.caption: Wooden pole tops compared by flag: Ireland, UK and France; the UK pole has a flat top

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: France, Ireland and the UK can be hard to tell apart. Look at the tops of wooden poles: UK ones are flat.

differs.how: Irish wooden pole tops are slanted

clues.title: Kerb: striped kerbs on main roads
text: Striped kerbs can sometimes be seen along main roads.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: On the Isle of Man, striped kerbs can sometimes be seen along main roads.

clues.title: Coverage: London - Gen 4 white electric vehicle
text: Some of the Generation 4 coverage in London and surrounding areas was taken by a white electric vehicle, with this distinct back of the car visible.
NOTE: A similar car was used in Dublin and Germany, so make sure to check out other clues as well.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bin: pink sticker, PEOPLE MAKE GLASGOW
text: This pink sticker with the text ''PEOPLE MAKE GLASGOW'' can be found on these trash bins in Glasgow.

images.caption: A bin with a city sticker; the sticker names a Scottish city

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A pink sticker saying PEOPLE MAKE GLASGOW is on trash bins in Glasgow.

clues.title: Guardrail: only A-type, no reflectors
text: UK only use A-Type guardrails which makes it useful to differentiate between Ireland and the UK.
NOTE: Ireland uses both A & B-Type.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Only A-type guardrails are used, which helps tell it from Ireland (A and B types).

differs.how: Ireland uses both A and B types

clues.title: Landscape: round hay bales on hilly fields
text: Cylindrical hay bales laying around on these hilly agricultural fields can mostly be found in the region north of Aberdeen. They can very rarely be seen elsewhere in Scotland.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Round hay bales lying on hilly farm fields are mostly found north of Aberdeen and very rarely elsewhere in Scotland.

clues.title: Wall: dark grey stone, upright top stones
text: Some roads, mostly in the south and north Snowdonia, have these distinct dark grey stone walls with vertical stones on top of it along the road. The landscape itself is very forested and mountainous, but less forested in the north east.
NOTE: These stone walls can be found elsewhere too, most commonly in North Wales.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In Snowdonia, mostly south and north, roads have dark grey stone walls topped with vertical stones. The area is forested and mountainous, less so in the northeast. Similar walls appear elsewhere in North Wales.

clues.title: Coverage: boat trekker
text: Boat trekkers are limited to three locations: the River Thames, which runs through London, Keyhaven Lake, and Loch Ness lake. Each have different boats and very different landscapes.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Boat coverage exists in only three places: the River Thames in London, Keyhaven Lake and Loch Ness. Each has a different boat and landscape.

clues.title: Phone numbers: area code 0141
text: Landline phone numbers in the UK always have nine or ten digits after the 0 trunk code. The first two to four digits after the 0 are the area code. Unfortunately for Geoguessr players, there is not much rhyme or reason to their geographic ordering.

However, the area codes of some large cities are still worth memorising. The most important ones are summarised in this infographic. Notably, all of Northern Ireland uses the phone code 028, and all of London uses 020.

clues.title: Houses: terraced hillside valley, pastel trim
text: This valley north-west of Cardiff has a very recognizable look. Featuring many terraced houses and brown stone walls with colorful windows and often have this unique shape made out of pastel around the windows and doors. The towns are build on hills so its always hilly.
NOTE: Similar valleys with the same look can be find elsewhere in Wales but this one is by far the biggest.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: The big valley northwest of Cardiff has many terraced houses, brown stone walls and colourful windows, often with pastel shapes around windows and doors. The towns are on hills. Similar valleys elsewhere in Wales are smaller.

clues.title: Pole: orange tape and white sticker with diamond
text: In Northamptonshire, you can often find orange tape wrapped around poles. A white sticker with blue text and numbers and a diamond shaped icon on it can commonly be seen aswell on the poles.

clues.summary: In Northamptonshire, orange tape is often wrapped around poles, plus a white sticker with blue text, numbers and a diamond icon.

clues.title: Sticker: colourful pole sticker
text: These colourful stickers are found in the Western Isles. Their very rarely seen since these islands are mostly rural without lampposts, but they can be seen commonly in Stornoway, and occasionally elsewhere too.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Colourful stickers in the Western Isles, rarely seen as there are few lampposts. They show up in Stornoway and occasionally elsewhere.

clues.title: Pole sticker: yellow, 6-digit code and QR code
text: This distinctive yellow sticker features a 6 number code followed by a QR code. This is a great clue that you are in the counties north of London. As it has consistently only been found in the following counties: Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex, Cambridgeshire, Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire. It is frequently found on rural wooden electricity poles.

images.caption: A yellow sticker with a 6-digit code and a QR code on a wooden pole

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A yellow sticker with a 6-digit code then a QR code, found on rural wooden poles in counties north of London: Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex, Cambridgeshire, Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire.

text: This busstop sign can be found in Greater Manchester, it has the phone code on it and the M logo on the top left corner with a bunch of other things like a bee on the right. The logo's and phone code can only be seen on one side.
NOTE: A different version can be seen in older coverage, which will be completely white with a huge M logo on it.

images.caption: Bus stop sign; the red arrow and circle point to the M logo at its top

clues.summary: The Greater Manchester bus stop sign has a phone code and an M logo top left, and a bee on the right, on one side only. Older ones are all white with a huge M.

clues.title: Landscape: wooded hills with towers to the west
text: Depending where you are in Belfast, you can often see these distinct mountains/hills with lots of trees on it (gets more bald on the top) to the west/north-west, sometimes with 1 or 2 towers on top of it. Hills can also be seen in the east/south east.
If your not sure these mountains are the Belfast mountains, check for clues to confirm your in Northern Ireland and it will 100% be Belfast.

clues.summary: In Belfast you often see wooded hills, balder on top, to the west and northwest, sometimes with one or two towers, and hills to the east and southeast. Once you know it's Northern Ireland, it is certainly Belfast.

clues.title: Landscape: treeless grassy hills, no mountains
text: You can recognize the Shetland Islands by the very low amount of vegetation and useally no trees at all. Patches of trees can rarely be seen on these islands. You will never see mountains either, its all just hills with mostly grass and some small bushes. Some parts also look like the Faroe Islands.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: The Shetland Islands have very little vegetation, usually no trees, no mountains, only grassy hills with small bushes. Some parts look like the Faroe Islands.

clues.title: Pole sticker: yellow with LCC under the numbers
text: Yellow stickers with ''LCC'' (which stands for ''Lincolnshire County Council'') written under the numbers can be found in Lincolnshire. ''LCC" can sometimes be hard to see, if you only see ''CC" clearly, that also confirms your in Lincolnshire.
NOTE: This doesn’t apply to North Lincolnshire and North East Lincolnshire (Scunthorpe, Grimsby and surrounding areas) which are separate councils.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Yellow stickers with LCC (Lincolnshire County Council) under the numbers mean Lincolnshire. If only CC is clear, that also confirms it. North Lincolnshire and North East Lincolnshire are separate councils.

clues.title: Pole sticker: white, FAULT and phone number
text: This white sticker with a black letter and 4 numbers, and has "FAULT'' with a phone number written under it is found in Perth and Kinross. Most of the times, it has a small frame in the sticker around the text.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A white sticker with one black letter and four numbers, and FAULT with a phone number below, is found in Perth and Kinross, usually in a small frame.

clues.title: Pole sticker: white with diamond and small text
text: This white sticker with black letters and numbers and a diamond with small text under it is found in Cambridgeshire, Coventry, Derby and South Tyneside.
Cambridgeshire + Coventry have 6 or less letters/numbers and white space between the text and diamond.
Derby always has 7 letters/numbers and no space between the text and diamond.
South Tyneside always has a blue sticker under it.
NOTE: This excludes Peterborough which has its own sticker, which always has ''PCC" written on a white sticker.

images.caption: Pole stickers from different UK areas, each labelled with its region name

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A white sticker with black letters and numbers and a diamond with small text underneath is found in Cambridgeshire, Coventry, Derby and South Tyneside. Derby always has 7 characters and no gap; South Tyneside has a blue sticker beneath; Peterborough has its own PCC sticker.

clues.title: Landscape: lots of sheep in hilly hedged fields
text: Sheep are most common in Wales, but can be found elsewhere too. So if you see a bunch of sheep and its very hilly/mountainous with typical Wale-ish landscape, with many hedgerows and green grassy fields and you have no other clues, you might aswell guess Wales.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Sheep are most common in Wales but can be anywhere. Lots of sheep in hilly or mountainous land with hedgerows and green fields is a fair guess for Wales.

clues.title: Houses: Tudor black-and-white timber
text: Tudor architecture, mostly black and white, sometimes with red bricks mixed are mostly found in West Midlands and East Anglia. They can also be found in Wales, mostly towards the England border. They can also be quite common in the south like Kent and Sussex and sometimes parts of Surrey and Oxfordshire. They can very rarely be found in Northern England and almost never in Scotland.

clues.summary: Tudor-style black-and-white buildings, sometimes with red brick, are mainly in the West Midlands and East Anglia, near the Welsh border, and fairly common in the south (Kent, Sussex, parts of Surrey and Oxfordshire). Rare in northern England, almost never in Scotland.

clues.title: Wall: very hilly national parks with stone walls
text: The Lake District, North Pennines, Yorkshire Dales, Nidderdale and Peak District are very hilly and have alot of stone walls. Stone walls can appear in other national parks and places but not as much as these 5 national parks, which have the majority of stone walls.

The Lake District is by far the hilliest, with plenty of exposed rock. Along with the North Pennines and Yorkshire Dales, it sometimes features abandoned-looking barns. Beyond that, I’m not sure how to tell them apart.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: The Lake District, North Pennines, Yorkshire Dales, Nidderdale and Peak District are hilly with most of the stone walls. The Lake District is the hilliest with bare rock; it, the North Pennines and the Dales sometimes have abandoned-looking barns.

clues.title: Pole sticker: blue stickers
text: Blue stickers/stickers with blue in them (excluding blue letters/numbers) are found in North Wales.
If you want, you can learn which blue stickers are found in which region:
Light blue stickers are found in Anglesey.
Green white dark blue stickers are found in Denbighshire.
Purple white light blue stickers are found in Conwy.
Generic blue stickers are found in Flintshire, Wrexham and Gwynedd, they are very rare in Gwynedd and are mostly found in Flintshire and Wrexham (east part of North Wales).
Other blue stickers can also be occasionally seen in North Wales.

clues.summary: Stickers with blue (not just blue text) are in North Wales: light blue in Anglesey, green-white-dark blue in Denbighshire, purple-white-light blue in Conwy, generic blue in Flintshire, Wrexham and rarely Gwynedd.

clues.title: Wall: castle-like stone walls
text: Stone walls that look like a castle wall are mostly found in North Wales. Especially towards Anglesey and in Anglesey. They can also sometimes be found elsewhere in Wales.

clues.summary: Stone walls that look like castle walls are mostly in North Wales, especially on and towards Anglesey, and sometimes elsewhere in Wales.

clues.title: Landscape: small hilly area, rock walls
text: This small region all the way south of ''mourne area of outstanding natural beauty'' features slightly hilly landscape with lots of rockwalls and distinct mountains to the north, further west there will be hedgerows instead of rockwalls but the same mountains can still be seen.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A small region at the far south of the Mournes area is slightly hilly with lots of rock walls and distinct mountains to the north. Further west there are hedgerows instead of walls but the same mountains.

clues.title: Landscape: very flat with big hedgerows
text: It is very common to see big hedgerows in north eastern Anglia, combined with its very flat landscape, most likely will be around that area.
NOTE: Its also common to see just normal hedgerows in this region, having normal hedgrows with flat landscape is still a good clue for this region.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Big hedgerows with very flat land point to north-eastern East Anglia. Normal hedgerows with flat land are also a good clue.

clues.title: Pole sticker: black eagle logo on top

clues.summary: A unique sticker with a black eagle logo on top is found in Bedford and around it.

clues.title: Landscape: hills with few mountains
text: Within the Scottish Highlands, the northern part of it is much less mountainous than the rest of the highlands. It has mostly just hills, with sometimes a few or less mountains visible in the distance.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: The northern Highlands are much less mountainous than the rest, mostly hills, with a few or no mountains in the distance.

clues.title: Language: English
text: English is the main language of the United Kingdom (I bet you knew that already). Keep in mind that English is also spoken in Ireland, aswell as Malta and Gibraltar within Europe. It is not uncommon to find English in other countries aswell, where is acts as an international language.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: English is the main language. It is also spoken in Ireland, Malta and Gibraltar in Europe.
